title: Explain that a fraction only makes sense for one whole cut into equal parts

lesson.title: One Whole, Equal Parts

steps.say: You already know how to cut a shape into equal parts and name the top and bottom numbers of a fraction. Today we answer a sneaky question: one half of what? A fraction only tells the whole story when we know which whole we cut, and that the pieces are the same size.

Here is the big idea. A fraction is always a piece of one whole, and that whole must be cut into equal parts. Look at this bar cut into four equal parts with one part shaded. Because all four parts are the same size, we can honestly call the shaded piece one quarter of the bar.

visual.caption: Four equal parts, one shaded, so one quarter

steps.say: Now the first tricky mistake. Imagine at the school picnic there is a giant party pizza and a small personal pizza. Someone says one quarter is always smaller than one half. But look, one quarter of the giant pizza is a big piece, and one half of the tiny pizza is a small piece. Fractions only compare fairly when they come from the same size whole.
steps.math: \frac{1}{4}\ \text{of a big pizza} > \frac{1}{2}\ \text{of a small pizza}

visual.caption: Big pizza one quarter versus small pizza one half

steps.say: Here is the second tricky mistake. Suppose I chop a granola bar into four pieces, but one giant chunk and three little slivers. Can I call the giant chunk one quarter? No I cannot, because the pieces are not equal. Cutting into four pieces is not enough. They have to be four fair, equal shares before the word quarter is allowed.

visual.caption: Only equal parts earn a fraction name

steps.say: So when you see a fraction, ask yourself two little questions. First, one whole of what? Second, are the parts equal? If a chocolate bar is cut into eight equal pieces and you eat three, you ate three eighths of that bar, and that number means three eighths of that bar only.

visual.caption: Three eighths of one chocolate bar

steps.say: So remember, a fraction always needs one whole, cut into equal parts, and it only makes sense when we know which whole we mean.
steps.headline: One whole, equal parts, and we know which whole

lesson.answer: A fraction only makes sense for ONE whole cut into EQUAL parts — always ask ‘a fraction of what?'

practice.question: Draw two fraction bars, one under the other. Make the top bar a long 30 centimetre licorice rope cut into four equal parts, and shade one part. Make the bottom bar a short 10 centimetre licorice rope cut into two equal parts, and shade one part. Maya says the top shaded piece is one quarter and the bottom shaded piece is one half, so the bottom piece must be bigger. Is Maya right? Explain why.
practice.answer: No. One quarter of the 30 centimetre rope is 7.5 centimetres, but one half of the 10 centimetre rope is only 5 centimetres, so the top piece is actually bigger. Maya compared fractions from two different wholes. Fractions only compare fairly when they come from the same size whole.
